1:
The psalm is dated by its ending. Calvin reasons that it "was written long after the death of David", since the close celebrates the kingdom erected in David's family and sets rejected Ephraim against it — from which "it is evident, that the ten tribes were at that time in a state of separation". Clarke reaches the same bracket: not David's, but "after the separation of the ten tribes... and before the Babylonish captivity, for the temple was still standing". Both report the same conjecture, that it belongs to the reign of Asa. Delitzsch notes only that "the old Asaphic origin of the Psalm has been contested", and observes the join with the psalm before: there Israel is a flock led by Moses and Aaron, here by David.

What kind of composition it is follows from the title. Delitzsch takes Maskil for "a meditation", the word being "also appropriate here in the signification a didactic poem". Henry agrees: "it is indeed Maschil, a psalm to give instruction; if we receive not the instruction it gives, it is our own fault." Augustine reads more into it: the inscription requires "a reader who doth perceive not the voice which the surface uttereth, but some inward sense."

The parable and the dark sayings are the tile's chief question, and nobody thinks them obscure. Henry says so directly: "these are called dark sayings, not because they are hard to be understood, but because they are greatly to be admired and carefully to be looked into." Wesley shifts the difficulty from the words to the facts — it is "God's transcendent goodness, their unparallel'd ingratitude" that are "prodigious and hard to be believed". Clarke keeps it plainer, taking the Hebrew for "example, as opposed to law or precept".

Augustine and Spurgeon take the same words as a warning against reading quickly. Augustine distinguishes them — a parable "hath on the surface thereof the similitude of something", while propositions "are questions having something therein which is to be solved by disputation" — and asks, "what man then would read parables and propositions cursorily?" Spurgeon defends the principle: "analogies are not only to be imagined, but are intended by God to be traced... the tribes and their marchings are living allegories."

Who claims a people divides them. Gill hears Christ, "King of the Jews, though they would not have him reign over them". Henry allows either David, who as king "would interpose his royal power for the edification of his people", or the psalmist as prophet speaking "as God's mouth"; Ellicott says only that the phrase points "to a position of weight and authority". On the second noun Ellicott and Wesley agree that "my law" is "rather instruction, or doctrine", where Henry keeps the stronger word: "every good truth, received in the light and love of it, will have the power of a law upon the conscience." Spurgeon asks the plain question: "shall God speak, and his children refuse to hear?"

Why a poem should carry the history is answered by Clarke from the state of the arts: "in those ancient times there was very little reading, because books were exceedingly scarce; tradition was therefore the only... means of preserving the memory of past events... handed down from father to son by parables or pithy sayings and by chronological poems." Ellicott makes the transmission a command rather than a custom, taking the relative as temporal: God "established it as a testimony in Jacob and as a law appointed it in Israel when he commanded our forefathers to make them known to their children." Wesley ranks that establishing first "as the chief of all his mercies", the testimony being so called "because it is a witness between God and men, declaring the duties which God expects from man, and the blessings which man may expect from God".
9:
Ephraim's turning back has no agreed occasion, and the search for one is what Ellicott sets out to abolish. Henry and Wesley both refer it to the Philistine rout in Eli's day, when the ark was taken; Wesley adds that Ephraim here "is put for all Israel". Clarke lists the alternatives and refuses to choose: "to what defeat of the Ephraimites this refers is not certainly known."

Ellicott proposes that there is no defeat in the verse at all. The literal Hebrew gives "drawing and shooting with the bow", but comparison with a later verse of the same psalm suggests instead "The sons of Ephraim are like men drawing slack bowstrings which turn back in the day of battle" — the turning back being the recoil of a bow, not a retreat of soldiers. He illustrates it from European history, where a battle "was determined at the outset by a shower of rain which relaxed the strings of our enemy's bows", and notes what the reading saves: "we are freed from the necessity of conjecturing a particular incident to account for this verse, which seems to break the sequence of thought." He then explains why the verse sits where it does: "the whole historical retrospect is intended to lead up to the rejection of the northern kingdom, but the poet is unable to keep back his climax, and thrusts it in here almost parenthetically."

Wesley reads the same structure without the philology: the psalmist, having stated the disaster, "falls into a large discourse of the causes of it", and only much later "returns to this history, and relates the sad consequence of that disaster, the captivity of the ark".

Henry finds the moral in the failure of equipment. The tribe was "well armed as ever" and yet "turned back when they came to face the enemy": "weapons of war stand men in little stead without a martial spirit, and that is gone if God be gone. Sin dispirits men and takes away the heart." He traces the cowardice to covenant-breaking and ingratitude, and orders them: "our forgetfulness of God's works is at the bottom of our disobedience to his laws." Gill measures how quickly the forgetting came — not in the next generation only but "in a few days, when they had been but three days' journey in the wilderness". Henry sees the narrative that follows as "a kind of struggle between God's goodness and man's badness", in which "mercy, at length, rejoices against judgment".

On the field of Zoan the geographers agree and disagree by degrees. Ellicott identifies it as "the classical Tanis, merely a corruption of Tsoan, i.e., low country", with "a rich plain known as the marshes, or the pastures, or the field of Zoan" stretching beside it. Clarke calls Tanis "the capital of Pharaoh, where Moses wrought so many miracles", while reporting an authority who took Zoan for Egypt at large. Ellicott also flags the psalm's method: it "now turns to the adventures in the wilderness, postponing the marvels in Egypt".

The water from the rock draws the tile's oddest suggestion. Ellicott renders the clause "oceans of drink", calls it "a poetical exaggeration", and then wonders whether more is meant: "or are we rather to think of the gift of water as produced by striking or boring through the rock to the great ocean on which the earth was supposed to rest?" He also separates two Hebrew words the English blurs, one always used of the event at Kadesh, the other of the rock at Horeb. Gill takes the two rocks as real places, "both to be seen at this day", and reads the guiding cloud as a type of Christ, "a shadow and security from the heat of a fiery law". Wesley makes the water pursue its drinkers, the streams having "miraculously followed them in all their travels, even to the borders of Canaan".
17:
The aggravation is the setting. Wesley notes that the sinning happened in the wilderness, "where they had such singular obligations to obedience"; Ellicott points out that the discontent was not new even then, having "already shown itself before the miraculous supply of water".

What they asked for is weighed by the word used. Clarke renders the request literally as meat "for their souls, i.e., for their lives", the complaint being that "the light bread, the manna, was not sufficient to sustain their natural force", and concludes: "they were wholly carnal... earthly, animal, and devilish." Wesley distinguishes need from appetite — the demand was "not for their necessary subsistence, but out of an inordinate and luxurious appetite" — and Gill locates the offence earlier, in the tempting of God "in their heart".

Gill then reconstructs the argument they made, and it is a piece of naturalism. Granting that the rock was struck and the water came, they suggested that the waters "might have been in the caverns of it before... and might have come out of themselves; and therefore this was no such great matter." Clarke draws the harder conclusion: "after all the miracles they had seen, they were not convinced that there was a Supreme Being!" — and turns it on the present: "their descendants in the present day are precisely in this state." Gill puts the offence formally: "faith gives glory to him, unbelief reflects dishonour upon him; faith sets its seal to him as true, but unbelief makes him a liar."

On the manna Gill offers two derivations — from a root meaning to prepare and distribute, or from the question "what is it?" the people asked at first sight — while Clarke explains "corn of heaven" physically: it fell "in the form of seeds", and appearing to come from the clouds "was not improperly termed heavenly corn". Wesley makes that heaven "a store-house, whereof God shuts or opens the doors."

Whose bread it was is the sharpest small dispute. Wesley takes the received "angels' food", the manna being "so called, because it was made by the ministry of angels". Clarke and Gill both prefer "the bread of the mighty ones", meaning "such bread as could only be expected at the tables of the rich and great" — and Gill draws the levelling consequence, that "the common people of Israel ate the same as their princes and nobles did". Ellicott reports the same alternative and declines to press it: "in connection with food from heaven, the popular idea of angels' food which poetry reluctantly gives up may be retained." Clarke supplies the irony either way: "how little did this gross people know of the sublime excellence of that which they called light bread!"

The winds that brought the quails are read as record rather than ornament. Ellicott judges them "probably the very winds that brought the flights of quails, and not merely poetical details", and treats the quantity the same way: "no doubt there is poetical hyperbole here", yet the numbers still taken today make the figure less extravagant. Gill keeps the winds in service: they "are under the power and government of God", who "says to one, Go, and it goes".

The eating is judged before the punishment falls. Gill will not let the excess pass as appetite: "they eat to excess, not merely to satisfy nature, but to gratify their sensual appetite: gluttony is a sin; it is an abuse of the creatures." How the wrath came he leaves open — "either by causing fire to come down from heaven, or by suffering them to be surfeited by excessive eating, or by sending a plague". Ellicott notes that the slain may be "either the strongest or the noblest"; Wesley chooses the first and finds the justice in it, the strongest being those who "probably were most desirous of this food, and fed most eagerly upon it."
32:
That neither kindness nor punishment worked is the point at which Clarke stops to marvel: "how astonishing is this! They were neither drawn by mercies, nor awed by judgments!" — before turning the astonishment on the reader, since "we shall cease to wonder at this, if we have a thorough acquaintance with our own hearts." Gill accounts for the failure of the mercies by their misuse: unless sanctified, they "often prove snares and temptations to sin yet more and more".

The punishment was slowness rather than slaughter. Gill notes that most were not cut off at once but "spent their time, for about eight and thirty years together, in fruitless marches to and fro", and draws the rule that "time spent in sin is all waste time". Clarke locates the vanity in the expectation itself, the people "vainly expecting an end to their labor, and the enjoyment of the promised rest, which, by their rebellions, they had forfeited".

What produced the repentance was fear, and they say so without softening it. Clarke describes the mechanism: "when they saw some fall, the rest began to tremble." Wesley makes the seeking urgent rather than sincere — they "speedily sought to God for ease and safety".

The titles they remembered are read as legal as well as devotional. Clarke presses the second hardest: the redeemer is "the strong God the Most High, their kinsman", one "who possessed the right of redemption; the nearest akin to him who had forfeited his inheritance". Ellicott traces the Rock to an older song of Moses; Wesley makes the recollection a discovery about resources, that God alone "had preserved them in all their former exigencies."

The flattery that followed is where the sharpest wording lies. Clarke thinks the Latin catches it best — "they loved him with their mouth; and they lied unto him with their tongue" — and quotes an old psalter: "thai sayde thai lufed God, bot thai lighed". His own comment is incredulity: "what idea could such people have of God, whom they supposed they could thus deceive?" Gill makes the same point from the Hebrew, which signifies attempting to deceive, and answers it: "he is not to be deceived, nor will he be mocked." Wesley calls the words "false protestations of their sincere resolutions of future obedience". Clarke states the principle underneath — "when the heart is wrong, the life is wrong" — and Gill describes that heart as "wavering, fickle, and inconstant... turning aside like a deceitful bow".

On the mercy that answered it, Ellicott makes a correction of tense that changes the sense. The verbs "should be in the present, But he, the compassionate, forgives iniquity, and doth not destroy" — turning a fact about one generation into a standing description of God. Clarke sharpens the verb instead: to forgive here is to have "made an atonement for their iniquity", and the restraint was real, since "he did not stir up all his wrath — the punishment was much less than the iniquity deserved." Gill finds the tenderness in the word for compassion itself, which comes from the same root as the word for the womb.

Why God relented divides on the meaning of one word. Gill offers two senses of flesh: either "poor, frail, weak, mortal creatures", or "naturally sinful and corrupt, prone to evil" — weakness in the one case, depravity in the other, and mercy in both. Clarke keeps the first and then objects to the English of the second clause: "I believe this to be a bad translation and may be productive of error; as if when a man dies his being were ended, and death were an eternal sleep." The Hebrew says something else — "the spirit goeth away, and it doth not return" — not that the man ceases, but that he does not come back to the probation he has left.
40:
"How oft" is answered with a number. Ellicott counts them: "ten instances of murmuring are actually recorded" in the books of Moses, and Gill notes that the Lord uses the same figure, the whole period coming to be named after the provocation. Henry makes the repetition itself the aggravation, and adds the asymmetry that gives the psalm its edge: "God kept an account how often they provoked him, though they did not."

Henry then distinguishes the two verbs: "by provoking him they did not so much anger him as grieve him, for he looked upon them as his children... and the undutiful disrespectful behaviour of children does more grieve than anger the tender parents." What grieved was not the insult but its consequence: "they put him under a necessity of afflicting them, which he did not willingly."

The word rendered "limited" is the tile's real difficulty, and neither philologist can settle it. Clarke reports the Chaldee, which has them "signed with a sign", and traces the root to a verb meaning to mark — the same from which the letter tau took its name, since "in the ancient Hebrew character" it "had the form of a cross X" and "was used as a mark". He concludes: "here it most obviously means an insult offered to God." Ellicott lays out the same field more coolly. The verb is used elsewhere "for putting a mark on the forehead, which has been very variously explained": some render "branded or cast a stigma on — i.e., brought discredit on the Divine name", the ancient versions have "exasperated", moderns offer "crossed" or "thwarted". His own resolution favours the simplest: "perhaps the ideas of marking something that has been tried, and that of trying or tempting are sufficiently near to allow us to render tempted."

Henry supplies the sense the English carries, and turns it into a rule. To limit God is to prescribe "what proofs he should give of his power and presence with them and what methods he should take in leading them", limiting him "to their way and their time". The presumption is answered out of the title: "being the Holy One, he will do what is most for his own glory; and, being the Holy One of Israel, he will do what is most for their good", so that in prescribing to him "we both impeach his wisdom and betray our own pride and folly."

Forgetting is the cause Henry assigns — the limiting was "occasioned" by "their forgetting his former favours" — and Spurgeon takes up the difficulty in it. Such displays "must have needed some more than usual effort to blot from the tablets of memory", so "it is probably meant that they practically, rather than actually, forgot", since "he who forgets the natural returns of gratitude, may justly be charged with not remembering the obligation." The day itself "was erased from their calendar, so far as any due result from it" — whence his observation that memory is "strange... in its oblivions as well as its records".

When the plagues arrive, Ellicott warns against reading them as a record: the reminiscence "is not a complete enumeration, and does not proceed in the order of the historic narrative." The details are handled economically. Gill finds the blood a matching penalty, "a just retaliation for drowning the infants of the Israelites in their river". Of the flies, Ellicott strips the adjective — "better, simply flies" — while Gill notes that the Hebrew signifies a mixture, and Wesley insists both flies and frogs "were doubtless extraordinary in their nature, and hurtful qualities". On the caterpillar Ellicott is least certain: it is "probably the locust in the larva or pupa state", though the versions render it "blight". Gill makes it "a kind of locust, and the same with the locust in the next clause", since the narrative names only the one.
47:
The vines raise a question about where the poet stood. Ellicott reports the objection: the plague narrative mentions neither vines nor sycamores, "and some consider that the poem reflects a Palestinian rather than an Egyptian point of view." He then dismantles it from the monuments: there is "abundance of evidence of the extensive cultivation of the vine in Egypt. The mural paintings contain many representations of vineyards", wine "stood prominent among the offerings to the gods", and a papyrus records rations of it. Clarke supplies the same fact: though the vine "was never plentiful in Egypt", the wine made there "is among the most delicious", and the sycamore was indispensable, "all their coffins" being "made of this wood".

Ellicott notices a variant that would change which plague is meant. Some copies read "pestilence" where the received text has hail, a reading he thinks "probably to be preferred though the authority of the LXX. is against it" — in which case the verse belongs to "the murrain that came on the cattle."

The evil angels puzzle all three. Clarke states the difficulty rather than solving it: "this is the first mention we have of evil angels. There is no mention of them in the account we have of the plagues of Egypt... and what they were we cannot tell." He infers their severity, since "by what the psalmist says here of their operations, they were the sorest plague that God had sent", and refuses to identify them with the destroying angel, which the psalm names separately. Ellicott removes the difficulty by removing the adjective: the Hebrew has "angels (or messengers) of ills", with "evident reference to the destruction of the firstborn". Wesley says only that they were those "whom God employed in producing these plagues".

The way made for the anger is measured, not merely opened. Ellicott renders the clause "levelled a path"; Gill hears a scale in it — "he weighed it in the balance of justice, and proportioned his anger to their crimes."

Against that stands the leading out. Gill makes the contrast turn on helplessness: the people went "like sheep, weak, timorous, unarmed", so that "it was not their arm, but his, that brought them out." Spurgeon presses the completeness of it: God "did not leave them halfway upon their journey; his power and wisdom preserved the nation till the palm trees of Jericho were within sight on the other side of the river."

What mountain is meant divides the three who ask. Ellicott takes it for Zion, "though from its apposition to border some prefer to take it of all the mountain country". Wesley takes the broader sense, "the word mountain" being "often used in scripture for a mountainous country"; Clarke agrees, drawing a contrast with where they had come from, since Canaan was "a mountainous country, widely differing from Egypt, which was a long, continued, and almost perfect level."

Settled, the children repeat the fathers. Henry states the cost: "presumptuous sins render even Israelites hateful to God's holiness. Those whom the Lord forsakes become an easy prey to the destroyer." The figure the psalm chooses for them brings Ellicott back to his earlier reading — "better, turned like a relaxed bow" — and he explains why it bites: Hebrew bows "were probably, when unstrung, bent the reverse way to that assumed when strung, which makes the figure more expressive of the disposition which cannot be relied upon in the moment of need." Clarke describes the same weapon from experience: such a bow "must be recurved, or turned the contrary way, in order to be... bent and strung", and if "a person who is unskilful or weak attempt to recurve and string one of these bows... it will spring back... and perhaps break his arm". Wesley keeps the plainer failure, a bow "which either breaks when it is drawn, or shoots awry, and frustrates the archer's expectation".
59:
The forsaking of Shiloh is read as final: God "gave up his ark into the hands of the Philistines", says Clarke, "and so true it is that he forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, that he never returned to it again." Ellicott identifies the occasion as "the disastrous defeat by the Philistines"; Wesley finds in the dwelling "among men" a double lesson, "both God's wonderful condescension, and their stupendous folly in despising so glorious a privilege", and explains the ark's two names: strength, "the sign and pledge of his strength put forth on his people's behalf", and glory, "the monument and seat of God's glorious presence".

The desolation is measured by silences. Clarke reads the maidens' fate as the absence of wedding music: they "were not celebrated with marriage songs", it being "a calamity in the east if a maiden arrives at the age of twelve years without being given in marriage." On the widows who did not mourn Ellicott is the most precise, referring it "undoubtedly" to the wife of Phinehas, who "died in premature labour, and so could not attend the funeral of her husband with the customary lamentations"; he prefers an old English rendering for catching it, "there were no widows to make lamentations." Wesley leaves it open, the widows "either prevented by their own death... or disturbed by the invasion".

The awaking is the boldest image in the psalm, and two of them say so. Clarke unpacks it without flinching: God had seemed "as if he had totally disregarded what was done to his people", and now rises "like a hero that shouteth by reason of wine". Ellicott registers the risk, ranking "the boldness of the image which likens God to a giant warrior exhilarated with wine" alongside one other picture in the Psalter. Gill supplies the moment of waking: "when he exerted his power in smiting the Philistines".

How the enemies were smitten "in the hinder parts" is agreed by two and hedged by one. Clarke and Gill refer it to the haemorrhoids that afflicted the Philistines while they held the ark; Ellicott allows also "the repeated defeats". Wesley finds the sharper irony: God "caused them to perpetuate their own reproach by sending back the ark of God with their golden emrods, the lasting monuments of their shame."

Ephraim's rejection is weighed against its record. Spurgeon sets out what the tribe had been — to it "belonged Joshua the great conqueror, and Gideon the great judge, and within its borders was Shiloh" — and why that ended: "sin had been found in them, folly and instability, and therefore they were set aside as unfit to lead." Judah's election is a fresh start.

What the sanctuary was built like produces four answers. Clarke reports that several versions took the Hebrew for the rhinoceros, the temple standing "as prominent on Mount Zion as the horn of the unicorn does upon his snout". Ellicott admits the clause "is vague" and guesses "perhaps, high as heaven — firm as earth". Wesley reads it as "magnificent and gloriously"; Gill takes it negatively, the sanctuary built unlike "the high places, where idolatry was committed". The ark, "before this time... frequently in a migratory state", was now fixed.

The shepherd king closes the psalm. Ellicott corrects the English of the flock — "ewes great with young" is "properly, ewes with lambs" — while Gill keeps the pastoral detail, the shepherd putting the sheep "before him" and following to drive them gently. Clarke notes that the promotion is not unparalleled, such instances being "not unfrequent in the ancient Greek and Roman history". On the last verse Clarke marks the close of a life — "here David is mentioned as having terminated his reign" — and Gill its character, since by his administration "he sought not his own honour and interest, but the good of his people."
